planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; let cut ends callus for a day or two before inserting to prevent rot.

directions: Native to Chiapas, Mexico, this small succulent shrub begins with erect fleshy stems that sprawl and become decumbent as the plant ages and lengthens. The narrowly obovate, yellow-green leaves taper to a short, sharp point and often blush red along the margins when grown in strong, direct sun. Terminal clusters of small white, star-shaped flowers open on bare stalks in spring. It is one of the parent species behind intergeneric Sedeveria hybrids such as 'Letizia', and like most Mexican sedums it needs gritty, fast-draining soil and a thorough dry-out between waterings to avoid rot.

planting.note: Grow in a small pot or enclosed terrarium with very high humidity (65-80%); this waterfall-spray-zone species struggles in open, dry household air and is best treated as a dedicated vivarium plant.

directions: Begonia microsperma is a compact West African species found from west Cameroon to Gabon, where it grows low to the ground in the humid spray zones of wet tropical forests. Its asymmetric, broadly ovate leaves have a pronounced puckered, bullate surface and a glossy medium-green color, with small yellow flowers held above the foliage on slender stalks. Give it bright, filtered light rather than direct sun, keep the growing medium evenly moist, and maintain humidity well above typical room levels, which is why it thrives best in an enclosed terrarium. It is one of the two wild parent species crossed to produce the popular hybrid Begonia 'Buttercup'.

planting.note: Pot in a sphagnum-based terrarium substrate and keep constantly moist to wet; this miniature species should never be allowed to dry out and does best in a closed, high-humidity vivarium.

directions: Endemic to the lowland rainforests of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, Begonia prismatocarpa is a tiny shrubby species that rarely exceeds a few inches tall, with red-tinged stems and bright yellow flowers streaked in reddish-orange that appear almost continuously. Keep the sphagnum or peat-based substrate constantly moist to wet, since this species resents drying out even briefly. Provide low to medium light rather than bright exposure, which tends to bleach the foliage pale, and favor an enclosed terrarium or vivarium setting over an open windowsill. It is one of the two wild parent species crossed to create the popular terrarium hybrid Begonia 'Buttercup'.
